19938.sum: Trent Viaducts are two adjacent parallel railway bridges which carry the Midland Main Line over the River Trent between Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire. Originally a single bridge, it was built by the engineer Charles Blacker Vignoles for the Midland Counties Railway in 1839. The Viaduct was rebuilt between 1891 and 1893 when a second crossing was added by the Midland Railway to carry the high-level goods line from Toton.

stories.text: Florence Boot, born in St Helier, Jersey, in 1863, married Jesse Boot in 1886 and helped him run the firm. She brought books and stationery into the Goose Gate shop and started Boots Book-Lovers' Library and cafés in the stores. She founded the university's first hall for women, named Florence Boot Hall after her.
Louisa May Long (1892–1981), who nursed with the 94 Nottingham VAD at Radcliffe on Trent in the First World War, was Matron of Florence Boot Hall from 1928 to 1946.

51735.sum: Florence Boot Hall is a student residence.

stories.text: A Georgian town house was built here in 1752. The Nottingham Subscription Library, founded in 1816, moved in during 1821. In 1836 a meridian line was laid so that the library's longcase clock could keep Nottingham time, 4 minutes and 33 seconds behind Greenwich, and it still does. In 1841 Alfred Barber opened the first photographic studio in the Midlands in its attics.
Edith Ransom (1872–1949) was the first woman president of Bromley House Library.
Ellen Harrington was the first woman librarian of Bromley House, from 1943 to 1983. Her portrait hangs here, in a room named after her.
George Green, the mathematician, was a miller: his family's windmill in Sneinton is restored and named after him.[^s1] He was a member of the subscription library at Bromley House.[^s1][^s2]

73862.sum: A library at Bromley House. The building was built in 1752, according to OpenStreetMap. It is Grade II* listed and was designed by Sir Robert Taylor.

stories.text: A legacy from the banker John Key paid for a hospital on part of Nottingham Park. Its first building, designed by John Simpson, was begun on 12 February 1781 and opened with 44 beds in September 1782; John Wesley was an early visitor. In 1844 it took in the hurt when a stand collapsed at a hanging on Garner's Hill, killing twelve. Hine added a storey in 1855, and Alfred Waterhouse's round Jubilee Wing opened in 1900. It closed in 1992, its work moved to the Queen's Medical Centre.

stories.text: On the night of 8–9 May 1941 the Luftwaffe bombed Nottingham. Firefighters saved St Mary's Church after an incendiary burned through its roof; three Boots factories, in Poplar Street, Island Street and Station Street, were on fire; University College and the Shakespeare Street chapel were hit. The worst loss was at the Co-op bakery on Meadow Lane, where 49 people died. In all, 159 people were killed that night.

Built in 1877–81 for University College Nottingham, with the town's library and a natural history museum, and damaged by bombs in the Second World War. D. H. Lawrence studied here to become a teacher; it is now Nottingham Trent University's Arkwright Building.

76264.sum: The Arkwright Building is a Grade II* listed university building on Shakespeare Street in Nottingham, England. It forms part of the Nottingham Trent University City Campus and is one of the university's principal historic buildings. Built between 1877 and 1881, the building was originally home to University College Nottingham, the city library and a natural history museum.

stories.text: Peter Mansfield came to the University of Nottingham in 1964 and developed magnetic resonance imaging here. Just before Christmas 1978 a full-body scanner was installed, and he made the first scan of a live patient. He shared the Nobel Prize in 2003 with Paul Lauterbur.

stories.text: George Thomas Hine designed the Nottingham Borough Lunatic Asylum, opened in August 1880 with its wards along one long corridor. It was extended in 1889, joined the NHS as Mapperley Hospital in 1948, and closed in December 1994. The north end is now Duncan Macmillan House, the local NHS trust's headquarters, and the south end, Nightingale House, is flats.

stories.text: The mill owner John Hawksley built a large cotton mill here, working before the end of 1791 with a 60-horsepower engine, and laid out Arnot Hill Park in about 1792 as a setting for his house. His son Thomas Hawksley, born at Arnot Hill House in 1807, became the engineer who gave Nottingham clean water. The house is listed Grade II.

The water engineer Thomas Hawksley was born at Arnot Hill House in 1807. His Trent Bridge waterworks, completed in 1831, gave Britain its first high-pressure constant supply, which kept dirty water out of the mains.

stories.text: In 1881–84 a pumping station was built here to raise drinking water for Nottingham from deep wells. It had two beam engines by James Watt & Co. and an engine house by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton, ornate with cast iron and stained glass. It pumped until 1969 and opened as a museum in 1976.

stories.text: Ibuprofen was first made at Boots in Nottingham in December 1961, by Stewart Adams's team. Their later laboratory, on Pennyfoot Street, is now BioCity, and in 2013 a Royal Society of Chemistry blue plaque marked the discovery.
Shortly after 1807 the baker George Green built a tower mill here. It burned in 1947, was restored and reopened in 1986, and is now part of a science centre.

300387.sum: Green's Windmill is a restored and working 19th-century tower windmill in Sneinton, Nottingham. Built in the early 1800s for the milling of wheat into flour, it remained in use until the 1860s. It was renovated in the 1980s and is now part of a science centre, which together have become a local tourist attraction.

stories.text: The Royalists of Newark raided again and again. Sir Charles Lucas broke into the town in January 1644 and tried to set it on fire, and in April 1645 a party from Newark took the fort at Trent Bridge. Each time Hutchinson won back what was lost, and each demand that he surrender the castle he answered with fresh defiance.

In 1947 the Trent flooded 3,000 properties, 86 factories and 28 miles of road in Nottingham, and the city's first flood defence was built that year. Photographs of West Bridgford under water are in Inspire Picture Archive. A new defence along 27 km of the river, from Sawley to Colwick, was finished in 2012.

stories.text: The medieval bridge had a chapel of St James at one end and was kept by a religious house, until on 21 February 1551 a royal charter passed its repair to the Corporation, with lands to pay for it, the Bridge Estate. Floods damaged it again and again, and in 1683 they swept away its northern half. Rebuilt with fifteen arches, 538 ft long in all, it stood until its foundations grew unsafe, and in the 1860s a new bridge was begun.

In 1156 a stone bridge of more than 20 arches was begun here. It was known as the Hethbeth bridge, and two of its arches survive on the south bank. The present iron bridge nearby was designed by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton, built between 1868 and 1871, and widened to 80 feet in 1924–26.

Marriott Ogle Tarbotton was Nottingham's Borough Engineer from 1859. He designed Trent Bridge, planned the town's underground sewers, culverted the River Leen and built the viaduct over the railway on Carrington Street in 1866.

303808.sum: Trent Bridge is an iron and stone road bridge across the River Trent in Nottingham, England. It is the principal river crossing for entrance to the city from the south, although the upstream Clifton Bridge is both larger and busier.
